newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's largest union group delays strike plans.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's largest union group delays strike plans.

text.p: South Korea's largest union organisation on Tuesday called on members to postpone a strike until January 11, a move that lifts the threat of a walkout by bank workers on Saturday, union officials said.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions (FKTU) is demanding the government withdraw a labour law rammed through parliament last week that gives companies the right to lay off employees, hire temporary workers and replace strikers.
A federation official, who declined to be named, said no specific date had been set for the resumption of the strikes.
"It will depend on the situation on January 11," she said.
In a statement, the federation said: "We are postponing the strikes in order to gather our strength for a longer, more determined struggle."

In response to the federation's call for a cooling-off period, the Korean Federation of Bank and Financial Workers' Unions said it would postpone a strike by bank tellers and clerks planned for Saturday.
Saturday is a half-day for most Korean workers.
The federation's move comes on the heels of a decision on Monday by the outlawed Confederation of Korean Trade Unions (KCTU) to postpone strikes over the New Year holidays.

The two umbrella groups claim an aggregate 1.7 million members in most of South Korea's major industries, including auto manufacturing, shipbuilding, and public sector services such as subways and hospitals.
The federation said it planned a second stage of strikes to be led by unions in the public sector.

"We will link the strikes to wage negotiations, work more closely with the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions and other citizens' coalitions, build stepping stones to work with the opposition parties and fight against the New Korea Party during next year's elections," the statement said.
The ruling New Korea Party of President Kim Young-sam pushed through the labour law at a clandestine session of the National Assembly on Thursday.
The militant KCTU has said it intends to resume walkouts after the New Year holidays.
Union workers at Daewoo Motor Co returned to work on Tuesday. Union officials said the union would meet on Friday to decide whether to resume industrial action.
Unions at other major automakers, including Ssangyong Motor, Hyundai Motor and Kia Motors, said on Tuesday they planned to continue stoppages.
On Monday, subway drivers returned to work after a two-day walkout, while nurses and hospital orderlies also agreed to resume their jobs.
